name: Internal bleaching

lead: Internal bleaching lightens a dark, root-canal-treated tooth, often at the front, so it matches the rest of the smile. The agent is sealed inside the tooth instead of applied to the outer surface.

Hydrogen peroxide, applied directly or produced from sodium perborate or carbamide peroxide, breaks down the pigment inside the tooth. A critical review reported over 90% immediate success, with 10 to 40% of treated teeth needing re-treatment within 1 to 8 years.

paras: The bleaching agent is replaced every few weeks over successive visits until the desired shade is reached. It is used for non-vital teeth, which lose their nerve supply and often darken.
Cervical root resorption is the main documented concern, linked especially to heated (thermocatalytic) methods. Dentine weakening and crown fracture have also been described.

angle.text: People with a single darkened root-canal-treated tooth, often at the front, use internal bleaching to match it to the rest of the smile. The bleach works from inside the tooth, and reports describe high immediate success with some re-treatment needed.

lead: Internal (intracoronal) bleaching is a tooth-whitening procedure for root-canal-treated, non-vital teeth, which lose their nerve supply and often darken [1][2]. The bleaching agent is sealed inside the tooth rather than applied to the outer surface, and is replaced every few weeks until the desired shade is reached; it is most often done on front teeth [2].

Present techniques rely on hydrogen peroxide, applied directly or produced from sodium perborate or carbamide peroxide [1]. A critical review reported more than 90% immediate success for intracoronal bleaching of non-vital teeth, with 10 to 40% of successfully treated teeth needing re-treatment over 1 to 8 years [1].
Cervical root resorption is the best-documented serious risk, linked especially to heated (thermocatalytic) methods [1][3][4].
infobox: Hydrogen peroxide, carbamide peroxide, sodium perborate

paras: In the walking bleach technique, a paste of sodium perborate and water or 3% hydrogen peroxide is placed in the pulp chamber and sealed between visits [4]. Discolouration of non-vital teeth can follow trauma, root canal materials or other causes; case reports describe darkening after white mineral trioxide aggregate and after triple antibiotic paste, and bleaching has been used to treat it [5][6].

The critical review reported over 90% immediate success and re-treatment need in 10 to 40% of cases during 1 to 8 years of follow-up [1]. An analysis of 255 teeth has also been published in the Australian Dental Journal [7].

Cervical root resorption is a possible consequence and is more frequent with thermocatalytic procedures; a 1984 report described external cervical resorption after bleaching a pulpless tooth [1][3][8]. A review of the walking bleach technique advised that heating the mixture is contraindicated because of resorption risk and formation of chemical radicals [4]. Wikipedia also notes intracoronal bleaching may damage dentine and lead to crown brittleness or fracture [2]. Studies have examined the effect of internal bleaching agents on dentinal permeability [9].

A registered trial evaluated intracoronal bleaching of primary anterior teeth after dental trauma in 13 children, with status listed as unknown [10]. The published literature is chiefly reviews, case reports and a retrospective analysis [1][4][7].

timeline.event: A report describes external cervical resorption after bleaching a pulpless tooth.[8]
Reviews of the biological aspects of bleaching and of the walking bleach technique are published.[1][4]
